 Supporters of Measure P react after seeing the first results of Marin County elections during a gathering Cafe Arrivederci in San Rafael, Calif. on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. From left are Joanne Webster, president and CEO of North Bay Leadership Council, Susan Gilmore, president and CEO of North Bay Children’s Center, Jenny Callaway, board secretary of Our Kids Our Future, and pediatrician Jessica Hollman. (Alan Dep/Marin Independent Journal) 
 By Dick Spotswood | spotswood@comcast.net PUBLISHED: November 10, 2026 at 12:59 PM PST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The Nov. 3 election provides lessons about Marin ballot measures to raise taxes: Form a coalition, make certain that its members vote, have a popular cause that’s easy to explain and include a sunset provision.
 Measure P supporters did just that. It authorizes an annual parcel tax of 5 cents per building square foot that sunsets in 15 years. The purpose was a literal motherhood issue: funding childcare and early childhood education.
 The measure was criticized for failing to explain in detail who’d receive the tax’s proceeds. That wasn’t an obstacle for voters frustrated by the high cost of childcare. Measure P was backed by parents, grandparents, liberals and, crucially, by Marin’s business community. The latter understood that providing affordable childcare was essential for recruiting and retaining top-flight employees.
 In early returns, P was trending to a 53.5% yes vote. A simple majority is required for passage.
 The same strategy worked in Mill Valley. So far, Measure T is achieving a landslide with 80% yes votes. It renews an annual tax of $303 per real estate parcel to fund on-going street repairs, wildland fire suppression and upgrading municipal facilities.
 It was backed by community leaders including united past mayors and by a public which saw and liked the tangible results that the municipal services tax had already delivered. It helped that the city indicated when this tax expires in 2038, it will not be renewed since the essential work will have then been accomplished.
 San Rafael civic leaders didn’t fare as well with Measure W. The proposal would have increased the tax paid on the sale of real property from 0.02% to 1%. Proponents showed that the City Council’s intent was to direct the measure’s proceeds to enhancing and guaranteeing continuance of public safety functions.
 The real estate sales industry was in opposition, contending that transfer-tax increases will increase the already staggering cost of homes. Measure W is going down to defeat with 60% opposed.
 There’s a lesson here for Novato Unified School District leaders. They desperately need additional funding to maintain existing educational programs. Another $6.5 million in budget cuts is soon projected. Novato Unified has already cut $14.3 million over the past three years.
 Another school tax measure is likely to be scheduled for this spring. Supporters should use the campaigns for measures P and T as templates to build a winning coalition and then get them to the polls.
 Measure X on Sausalito’s ballot wasn’t a tax measure. It’s solely related to zoning in the city’s Marinship neighborhood on Richardson Bay, the site of a long-gone World War II shipyard.
 Failing in preliminary returns with 65% of voters opposing, the measure was a reminder of an old rule. There’s one action in Marin that usually leads to defeat at the ballot box. That action is change.

 Land use in Marinship is governed by a decades-old law that essentially required any meaningful land use change to be approved via ballot box referendum. That complex and expensive process is not the law in most other Marin communities. It virtually guarantees that nothing substantial will ever change even to existing structures.
 Most Sausalitans have a romantic notion of Marinship as still being an old seaport with marine uses predominating. Let’s acknowledge that in most Marin towns and especially in rural West Marin, residents have similarly idealistic notions that they’ll passionately fight to preserve.
 While most Marin residents understand that some change is inevitable, the fear remains that any change will lead to negative consequences.
 There’s plenty of incidents where that’s been the upshot. Yet there’s also many communities that found new land uses that were beneficial for most residents. Exhibit One is Novato’s Hamilton Air Force Base, which transitioned into what is today a nationally admired planned residential community.
 Columnist Dick Spotswood of Mill Valley writes on local issues Sundays and Wednesdays. Email him at spotswood@comcast.net.
